なっとう を たべさせられた — I was made to eat nattō
You say what you were made (forced) to do against your will with the causative-passive ～させられる / ～される (たべさせられる, まき を わらされる, またされる) and tell it apart from ～させて もらう.
to be made to do (something unpleasant)
to leave (on your plate), to leave behind
At school lunch I was made to eat nattō.
As a child, my grandfather made me split firewood.
My mother makes me practise the piano every day (and I don’t like it).
Kenji kept me waiting for a whole half hour.
That film really made me think.
To form the causative-passive: たべる → たべさせられる, よむ → よまされる / よませられる, する → させられる, くる → こさせられる.
To understand the meaning: someone MADE YOU do something and YOU didn’t want to (“I was forced to…”).
To use the structure: [I] は [the one who makes] に [the thing] を ～させられる.
To tell a complaint (～させられた) apart from gratitude (～させて もらった / くれた).
To put all the forms of the unit side by side: active, passive, causative, causative-passive.

Early November, Saturday, nine in the morning in Bucharest (four in the afternoon in Hiroshima). Sakura calls on video, really sulky. Ana is sitting on the sofa wrapped in a blanket, and only her face shows on the screen.
Mihai, listen! Yesterday at school I was made to eat nattō!
What, nattō? You can’t stand nattō, right?
I hate it! But they say you’re not allowed to leave anything at school lunch. The teacher made me eat all of it.
You poor thing. Nattō has a strong smell. I got a fright too the first time I ate it.
And on top of that, when I got home, Mum made me practise the piano for an hour again. I wanted to play with my friends.
I was made to do all sorts of things when I was little, too. When I went to Grandpa’s village in the summer, he made me split firewood every morning.
About ten, I think. The axe was heavy and my hands hurt. And I was woken up at five and made to feed the chickens.
At five?! That’s harder than me!
But thanks to that, on our honeymoon Mihai split the firewood like a pro.
Yes. Back then I hated it, but now I’m grateful to my grandpa.
Hmm… Then maybe one day I’ll be glad about the piano too.
Of course. When I was little, my mum made me eat lentils every week too, and now I love them.
And you? Are you made to do something now too?
(Laughing) Right now… Mihai makes me go to bed early every evening. And he makes me drink milk.
Why? You’re like a little kid!
“nokosha dame” = you’re not allowed to leave
I was made to do; made to give
sa-se-ra-re-ru: five even syllables, don’t swallow any of them. Practise slowly, then fast: たべ-さ-せ-ら-れ-る.
nat-too: っ is a short pause before the “t” (like the gap in “hot-tub” said slowly), and とう has a long “o”.
kyuu-sho-ku, gyuu-nyuu: きゅ, ぎゅ, にゅ are each one single syllable; the “u” of う is lengthened.

In chapter 33 you learned the causative: SOMEONE makes you do something (はは は わたし に ピアノ を れんしゅう させる). Now we look at the same scene from the side of the person who is forced: I WAS MADE to do it. Japanese glues the causative (～させる) and the passive (～られる) into a single verb: ～させられる.
My mother made me practise the piano. (causative: mum is the subject)
I was made by my mother to practise the piano. (causative-passive: I am the subject)
In English we say “I was made to”, “they forced me to”, “I had to (like it or not)”. Japanese always adds a nuance: I DIDN’T WANT TO. It’s the typical form for complaining.
The order is always the same: first せ (causative), then られ (passive): たべ + させ + られる. There’s no such thing as “たべられさせる”.
You start from the causative (which is an ichidan verb) and make its passive: ～せる → ～せられる. Godan verbs also have a SHORT form, very common in speech: ～せられる → ～される.
The short form ～される exists ONLY for godan verbs, and NOT for those ending in す: はなす → はなさせられる (never “はなさされる”). For ichidan verbs, する and くる you only use the long form.
It conjugates like any ichidan verb: たべさせられる → たべさせられます, たべさせられた, たべさせられて いる, たべさせられない.
The person who is forced is the subject (は / が). The person who does the forcing gets に, as with the passive. The object keeps を:
As with the “suffering” passive (ch. 32), the person doing the forcing can be left out: きゅうしょく で なっとう を たべさせられた (at school lunch I was made to eat nattō; obviously by the teacher).
～させられて いる = I’m made to do something repeatedly, as a habit: まいにち ピアノ を れんしゅう させられて いる (every day I’m made to practise).

A few fixed expressions you’ll meet very often: またされる (to be kept waiting), かんがえさせられる (to be made to think: あの えいが には かんがえさせられた = that film really got me thinking), なかされる (to be moved to tears: あの はなし には なかされた).
Sometimes I actually wanted to do the thing, and the other person let me. Then you DON’T use ～させられる (it would sound like a complaint) but the causative + もらう / くれる (ch. 23 and 33):
I didn’t want to, I was forced
ちち に りゅうがく させられた (my father sent me to study abroad, against my will)
I wanted to, I was given permission
ちち に りゅうがく させて もらった (my father let me go and study abroad)
I wanted to, and I’m grateful
ちち が りゅうがく させて くれた (my father let me go, how kind of him)
I wanted to, but I wasn’t allowed
アニメ を みせて もらえなかった (they didn’t let me watch anime)

The same event can be told in two ways. Mihai at ten: まき を わらされた (I was made to). Mihai now: おじいちゃん が まき の わりかた を おしえて くれた (Grandpa taught me how to split firewood). In Japanese, the form shows how you feel.
The whole unit in one row. Look how the subject changes, and what they feel:
よまされる (I’m made to read)
たべさせられる (I’m made to eat)
Javier was made by Kenji to make ramen (and didn’t want to).
Javier was allowed by Kenji to make ramen (which is what really happened in ch. 33).
“I was made by my grandfather to split firewood.”
You WANTED to study abroad and your father let you. What do you say?
When I was little, my mother made me eat vegetables.
I was made by the teacher to read aloud.

Saturday evening in Hiroshima, after the call with Mihai and Ana, Sakura writes in her diary. Yesterday was not her day.
They served nattō at school lunch and the teacher made me eat all of it.
When I got home, Mum made me practise the piano for an hour.
When I called Dad, he was busy with the soup and kept me waiting for half an hour.
But today I talked on video, and it seems Mihai was made to split firewood when he was little too. It’s not just me, and that made me feel a bit better.
Why did Sakura wait half an hour?
Dad was busy with the soup
Why did Sakura feel better at the end?

こども の ころ の おもいで — Childhood memories
The next Saturday, Ioana came to Mihai and Ana’s flat at ten, as usual.
Today was a special day. She was going to talk to Sakura on video for the first time.
Ioana had been nervous since the morning and had rehearsed her Japanese greeting countless times.
Ana was sitting on the sofa, wrapped in a big blanket.
“Ana, are you cold?” Ioana asked, and Ana answered, laughing: “No. The house doctor is making me rest.”
Mihai brought warm milk and handed it to Ana. Ioana found it a little strange.
Sakura’s face appeared on the computer screen. In Hiroshima it was already five in the afternoon.
“Nice to meet you. I’m Ioana. I’m very pleased to meet you.”
“Nice to meet you! I’m Sakura. I’m nine. You’re the one who found Mihai’s wallet, right?”
“Yes. And thanks to it, I got to meet your photo.”
Sakura laughed happily. “Ioana, your Japanese is really good!”
Sakura immediately told the nattō story from the week before: how she’d been made to eat all of it at school lunch.
“Were you made to eat things you couldn’t stand when you were little, too?”
Ioana thought for a moment and laughed. “Me too. My grandma made me eat ciorbă de burtă.”
Mihai explained: “It’s a soup made from cow’s stomach. It’s very popular in Romania.”
“Cow’s stomach?!” Sakura’s eyes went wide. “I’d rather have nattō!”
Everyone laughed. Ana was laughing under the blanket too.
“But you know, now I love ciorbă de burtă,” said Ioana, and Sakura shouted: “No way!”
Ana said from under the blanket too: “My mum made me eat lentils as well, and now I cook them myself. Maybe the ‘I don’t like it’ of childhood turns into ‘I like it’ when you grow up.”
Now it was Ioana’s turn to tell a story.
“My mum made me practise my handwriting every evening. One page a day.”
“Until I finished, she wouldn’t let me watch cartoons. So there were days when I wrote crying.”
“But thanks to that, now I can write hiragana and kanji neatly. My teacher often praises me.”
Sakura said: “Show me!” When Ioana held her notebook up to the camera, Sakura whispered: “Nicer than my handwriting…”
“And what does your mum say now?” Sakura asked.
“She’s really happy that I’m learning Japanese. She says: ‘Finally those pages were good for something.’”
“What about you, Mihai? Besides the firewood, were you made to do anything else?”
Mihai laughed and told a story from when he was six.
“Grandpa made me carry the milk bucket. But I fell on the way and spilled all of it.”
“No. Grandpa didn’t say anything. The next morning he just made me carry the same bucket again.”
“This time I walked slowly, one step at a time. When I got home, Grandpa patted me on the head. I still remember how big his hand was.”
“By the end of the summer I could carry the bucket by myself. Then Grandpa made me a little stool.”
“That stool is still next to the stove in the house in the village. Ana sat on it on our honeymoon, too.”
Ioana listened quietly and wrote “motasareta” in her notebook. It was a new word.
At the end, Ioana asked: “Sakura, would you play something for me on the piano?”
Saying “Well, it’s the piece I’m made to practise every day,” Sakura sat down at the piano.
What came flowing out was an old Japanese song, “Sakura Sakura”.
The gentle melody filled the small room in Bucharest. Tears welled up in Ioana’s eyes.
“Why are you crying?” Sakura asked, worried.
“Because it was beautiful. Because you practised every day, I was able to hear this song now.”
Sakura was quiet for a while. Then she said, a little embarrassed:
“…Then I’ll practise tomorrow too. And this time not because I’m made to, but because I want to.”
After the call ended, Ioana said to Mihai: “When I was little, I hated being made to do things. But I feel that everything I am now comes from there.”
Mihai nodded. The hands that split firewood and the feet that walk slowly, one step at a time—he had got them from his grandfather.
“I think so too, Ioana. Maybe the firewood I was made to split back then is still keeping me warm now.”
Meanwhile, in Hiroshima, Haruka was secretly reading Sakura’s diary.
“Today Ioana cried listening to me play the piano. I don’t like practising, but now I like it a tiny bit.”
Haruka smiled and closed the notebook without saying anything.
In Bucharest, under the blanket, Ana was resting her hand gently on her belly. But nobody had noticed yet.

What you were made to do as a child

Write 8–10 sentences about the things you were made to do when you were little (at home, at school, at your grandparents’). How did you feel then, and what do you think now? Finish with something you were allowed to do and are grateful for.
I used the causative-passive at least 4 times (at least once the short form ～される).
I marked the person doing the forcing with に.
I used ～させて もらった or ～させて くれた once (gratitude).
I used a time word: こども の ころ, なつやすみ, まいにち.
When I was little, my mother made me clean my room every day.
In the summer holidays, my grandfather made me help him in the fields. It was very hot.
